title: Why Amadou Daffe's Developer Marketplace Began as a School
dek: In 2016 Amadou Daffe came back to Ethiopia to build a marketplace for African developers, and found it had to begin as a school.

story.event: Founding Gebeya and opening its developer-training academy in Addis Ababa
story.industry: education (software developer training and talent marketplace)
story.summary: In 2014 Amadou Daffe, at a Coders4Africa conference in Addis Ababa, promised the audience he would return to build a company; in 2016 he and Hiruy Amanuel, who met in Silicon Valley, founded Gebeya, a marketplace for African developers with a training academy in Addis Ababa. Facing Ethiopia's foreign-investment rules, months of licensing and too few freelance-ready developers, they made training the core of the business; the academy opened in September 2016 and its first cohort of seventy graduated in May 2017.
paragraphs: In 2014 Amadou Daffe came to Addis Ababa for a two-day conference run by Coders4Africa, the developer network he had co-founded. About 500 young people working in technology attended. Daffe, who has Senegalese roots, had grown up in three African countries before moving to the United States as a teenager. He later said he had never thought of Ethiopia as a technology country, and found the size of its young population daunting. By his own account, he promised the audience he would come back and build a company.

Two years later he was raising money for the idea, first called developer as a service, and still weighing Ethiopia against Kenya. In April 2016, in Silicon Valley, he met Hiruy Amanuel, an investor and entrepreneur of Ethiopian origin, who asked to join and invest. They named the venture Gebeya, Amharic for marketplace: an online market where vetted African developers would take on client projects, fed by an academy in Ethiopia aiming to train about 5,000 people in five years.

The obstacles were visible from the start. Both founders were American citizens, and Daffe said Ethiopian law required them, as foreign investors, to commit $200,000. Licensing took more than six months, he recalled, and they registered Gebeya in Kenya as well, "just in case it didn't work out." The harder problem was people: too few developers were ready for paid freelance work, so the school had to come before the market. "One of the biggest challenges was the training," he said. In the first eighteen months, he told an Ethiopian magazine, the founders put in almost half a million dollars.

The academy opened in September 2016, accepting seventy trainees after applications and interviews and offering women partial or full scholarships. On 20 May 2017, after about six months of hands-on training, the first cohort graduated onto Gebeya's marketplace; the company had launched in Kenya that January. That summer Daffe said more than 500 people had applied in four months.

Gebeya kept changing shape. A 2021 profile produced by the IFC reported about 800 people trained, roughly a third matched with employers, and more than $3.2 million raised. By 2023 it was moving towards supplying tools for other people's online marketplaces.

quote.text: May He (the Supreme Being) protect us both, teacher and taught. May He be pleased with us. May we acquire strength. May our study bring us illumination. May there be no enmity among us.
quote.source_title: The Upanishads, tr. Swami Paramananda, Project Gutenberg eBook #3283
quote.connection: Gebeya set out to be a marketplace and found it first had to be a school. The chant recited before Upanishadic study asks one blessing for teacher and taught together, as if strength and understanding reach both of them or neither.

reflection: Daffe's promise in that conference hall was the easy part. What took the money and the months was discovering that the people his market needed did not yet exist in enough numbers, and deciding to train them rather than wait. He also kept a second door open in Kenya, which was less a lack of faith than a way of keeping the first one possible.

You probably teach more than you count: the colleague you show a technique to, the student on attachment, the friend who asks how you managed something. That work rarely appears in a plan, yet a great deal rests on it, and the chant's point is that both sides are meant to come away stronger.
invitation: Think of one person who has learned something from you this year. Today, ask them what still confuses them, and listen to the whole answer before you offer to fix it.

research_notes: The slate's 'founding-decision' in 2016 holds. Timeline: Daffe's 2021 Loline interview puts his first visit to Ethiopia, and his promise to the audience, at a 2014 Coders4Africa conference; HapaKenya (August 2016) dates the Silicon Valley meeting with Hiruy Amanuel to April 2016. HapaKenya says Daffe went to Silicon Valley as CEO of Coders4Africa seeking investors to help C4A scale, while Condia (2023) says he exited C4A in 2015 and Loline says he was raising money for his new startup, DAAS; the story says only that he was raising money for the idea. Loline places the meeting in San Francisco; HapaKenya, Disrupt Africa and 2merkato say Silicon Valley; the story uses Silicon Valley. The cohort: 2merkato says the academy 'accepted seventy candidates'; Disrupt Africa and Daffe himself (Black Enterprise, July 2017) say 70 graduated. The story says seventy were accepted and that the first cohort graduated, without claiming that every trainee finished. Training length: 2merkato and Disrupt Africa say about six months (2merkato's own dates, September to 20 May, span about eight); Black Enterprise describes later programmes as four to six months. The $200,000 is Daffe's figure; Abyssinia Law confirms USD 200,000 as the general minimum for a single foreign investment project under the repealed law, with lower thresholds for joint ventures and some consultancy services, so the story attributes it to Daffe. 'Almost half a million dollars' in the first eighteen months comes only from the Loline interview and is attributed. Outcome figures: Black Enterprise (July 2017) quotes Daffe on over 500 applicants in four months and 140 professionals placed; the IFC profile (January 2021) gives about 800 trained, a third matched and over $3.2 million raised; Condia (2023) reports over $1 million revenue in 2018 (not used). No source contradicts these; each is dated and attributed in the story. Funding is set to 'mixed': the founding was paid for by the founders, Amanuel joining as co-founder and investor, and later growth came from outside investors. The Loline interview is written partly in paraphrase; the two short quotations used ('just in case it didn't work out' and 'One of the biggest challenges was the training') are given in quotation marks there and attributed to Daffe. The Peace Chant is the invocation that opens the Katha-Upanishad in Paramananda's translation (the same chant traditionally recited by teacher and pupil before study); the parenthesis is the translator's.
